title: Γυναῖκες ἀμφ’ αἷμα
titleEn: The Women at the Pit — Odyssey 11.210–320
about: Odysseus, still telling the Phaeacians his story, answers his mother’s shade at the pit of blood in the land of the dead. He asks why she will not let him embrace her, and she explains that the dead are no longer flesh and bone, only a soul that flits like a dream, and tells him to go back to the light and remember it all for his wife. Then Persephone sends up the wives and daughters of the great men of old, and Odysseus lets them drink the blood one at a time and asks each who she is. He names them in turn: Tyro, loved by Poseidon in the shape of a river, and her sons; Antiope and the founders of Thebes; Alcmene and Megara, the mother and wife of Heracles; Epicaste, who married her own son and hanged herself; Chloris and the story of the cattle her daughter Pero cost; Leda and her two sons, who live and die in turn; and Iphimedeia, whose giant sons Otus and Ephialtes threatened to pile mountains up to heaven and were killed by Apollo before they grew beards.

sentences.l:
‘Mother mine, why, then, do you not wait for me, eager to seize you,
that even in Hades’ (house), our dear arms around each other having thrown,
we two may take our fill of chilling lament?
sentences.i: ‘Mother, why do you not wait for me, when I am eager to take hold of you, so that even in the house of Hades we two may throw our dear arms about each other and take our fill of chilling lament?
sentences.n: Odysseus’ own words to his mother begin here, the speech introduced at the end of the last part; he is still telling the tale begun in book 9, so his words are in single quotation marks. μίμνεις is ‘you wait’ (μίμνω, a reduplicated form of μένω). ἑλέειν is the aorist infinitive of αἱρέω, ‘to seize’, with its vowels left open, and μεμαῶτα, the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, agrees with the μ’ (‘me’) before it. In περὶ … βαλόντε the preposition stands apart from its participle (tmesis); βαλόντε and ἀμφοτέρω are dual forms, ‘we two’. τεταρπώμεσθα is a reduplicated aorist subjunctive of τέρπω, ‘take one’s fill of’, in a purpose clause after ὄφρα. εἰν is ἐν, with ‘house’ understood after Ἀίδαο; κρυεροῖο ‘chilling’ is from κρύος ‘frost’.

sentences.t:
ἦ τί μοι εἴδωλον τόδ’ ἀγαυὴ Περσεφόνεια
ὤτρυν’, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὀδυρόμενος στεναχίζω;
sentences.l:
Can it be that this phantom, to me, noble Persephone
has roused, so that still more, lamenting, I may groan?’
sentences.i: Can it be that noble Persephone has roused this phantom for me, so that I may groan still more, lamenting?’
sentences.n: Odysseus asks whether this is his mother at all, since he could not hold her. ἦ opens the question, ‘can it be that …?’; τί is left untranslated here; it may be the adverbial ‘at all’ or ‘really’. εἴδωλον is a ‘phantom’, a mere likeness of a person. ὤτρυν’ is ὤτρυνε, ‘roused, sent’, from ὀτρύνω; Persephone is the queen of the dead, and ἀγαυή is the ‘noble’ of ‘the noble suitors’. στεναχίζω, after ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον ‘so that still more’, is a subjunctive (the first-person form is the same as the present indicative); ὀδυρόμενος is ‘lamenting’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμείβετο πότνια μήτηρ·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she then at once answered, the lady mother:
sentences.i: So I said, and my lady mother answered me at once:
sentences.n: Odysseus the narrator again, introducing his mother’s answer. The line is the one at 11.180 and has the English it already has there. ἐφάμην is the middle imperfect of φημί, ‘I spoke’; ἀμείβετο is ‘answered’, the imperfect without its augment (Attic ἠμείβετο); πότνια is ‘lady’, a title of honour (it is also used of goddesses), here given to his mother. The speech was closed in the unit before, so this line carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι, τέκνον ἐμόν, περὶ πάντων κάμμορε φωτῶν,
οὔ τί σε Περσεφόνεια Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἀπαφίσκει,
ἀλλ’ αὕτη δίκη ἐστὶ βροτῶν, ὅτε τίς κε θάνῃσιν·
sentences.i: ‘Oh me, my child, ill-fated man beyond all men, Persephone, the daughter of Zeus, is not deceiving you at all, but this is the way of mortals whenever one of them dies:
sentences.n: His mother’s answer; her speech, in single quotation marks, runs to the end of line 224. ὤ μοι is a cry of distress, ‘oh me’. κάμμορε is a vocative, ‘ill-fated one’, built on μόρος ‘portion’ (a doubled μ, from κατά taken into the word); περὶ πάντων … φωτῶν is ‘beyond all men’, with φώς ‘man’ and περί meaning ‘beyond’. Διὸς θυγάτηρ is the stock ‘daughter of Zeus’, and ἀπαφίσκει is ‘deceives’. δίκη means ‘way, custom’ here, not ‘justice’; βροτῶν is ‘of mortals’. ὅτε … κε θάνῃσιν is a general statement, ‘whenever someone dies’, with κε and an aorist subjunctive.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτι σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα ἶνες ἔχουσιν,
ἀλλὰ τὰ μέν τε πυρὸς κρατερὸν μένος αἰθομένοιο
δαμνᾷ, ἐπεί κε πρῶτα λίπῃ λεύκ’ ὀστέα θυμός,
ψυχὴ δ’ ἠύτ’ ὄνειρος ἀποπταμένη πεπότηται.
sentences.l:
for no longer flesh and bones do the sinews hold,
but these, as always, the strong strength of burning fire
overpowers, when first the life has left the white bones,
and the soul, like a dream, having flown away, flits about.
sentences.i: For the sinews no longer hold flesh and bones, but the strong strength of burning fire overpowers them as soon as the life has left the white bones, and the soul flies off like a dream and flits about.
sentences.n: Anticleia explains why there is nothing to hold: the body is burned and the soul flies off. ἶνες is ‘sinews’ (ἴς, pl. ἶνες). τὰ μέν τε is ‘these’ (the article-form is a pronoun) with epic τε, marking a general truth; the contrast comes with ψυχή in line 222. πυρὸς … αἰθομένοιο is ‘of burning fire’; κρατερὸν μένος is ‘strong strength’, two different words (κρατερός ‘strong’, μένος ‘strength’), and the English keeps both. δαμνᾷ is ‘overpowers’, a present of δαμνάω (= δάμνημι). ἐπεί κε … λίπῃ is ‘as soon as … has left’, with κε and an aorist subjunctive. θυμός here is the life that leaves the bones, not the heart that feels. ψυχή is the soul, apart from the body. ἠύτ’ is ἠύτε ‘like’; ἀποπταμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἀποπέτομαι ‘fly away’, and πεπότηται the perfect of ποτάομαι ‘flit about’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ φόωσδε τάχιστα λιλαίεο·
sentences.l: But toward the light as quickly as possible long to go;
sentences.i: But be eager to reach the light as quickly as you can;
sentences.n: Her talk turns from what happens to the dead to advice for the living. φόωσδε is ‘to the light’: φόως is an epic form of φάος ‘light’, and -δε is the suffix of direction. λιλαίεο is the imperative of λιλαίομαι ‘long for, be eager’, in the uncontracted form -εο (Attic -ου). τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’. The unit stops in the middle of line 223, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δὲ πάντα
ἴσθ’, ἵνα καὶ μετόπισθε τεῇ εἴπῃσθα γυναικί.
sentences.l:
and these things all
know, so that even afterward you may tell your wife.’
sentences.i: and keep all this in mind, so that later you can tell it to your wife.’
sentences.n: ταῦτα … πάντα is ‘all these things’, the object of ἴσθ’, which is ἴσθι, the imperative of οἶδα ‘know’; ‘know all this’ means ‘take note of it, remember it’. ἵνα καὶ … εἴπῃσθα is ‘so that also … you may tell’, a purpose clause; εἴπῃσθα is a second-person subjunctive of εἶπον in an old form with the ending -σθα. τεῇ is ‘your’, the epic possessive τεός (Attic σός); the wife is Penelope, though she is not named. μετόπισθε is ‘afterwards, later’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
νῶι μὲν ὣς ἐπέεσσιν ἀμειβόμεθ’, αἱ δὲ γυναῖκες
ἤλυθον, ὤτρυνεν γὰρ ἀγαυὴ Περσεφόνεια,
ὅσσαι ἀριστήων ἄλοχοι ἔσαν ἠδὲ θύγατρες.
sentences.l:
We two thus with words were exchanging answers, and the women
came, for noble Persephone had roused them,
as many as were wives of the best men and daughters.
sentences.i: So the two of us were answering one another with words, and the women came, for noble Persephone had roused them, all who were wives and daughters of the best men.
sentences.n: A new paragraph and a new scene: the other dead women come up. The narrator is Odysseus again, so the quotation marks are closed. νῶι is the dual ‘we two’ (Odysseus and his mother); ἀμειβόμεθ’ is ἀμειβόμεθα, ‘we were answering one another’, with ἐπέεσσιν ‘with words’ (the dative ending -εσσι). ἤλυθον is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι, ‘they came’. ὤτρυνεν γάρ gives the reason: Persephone had roused them, as Odysseus asks in 213 whether she had roused the phantom. ὅσσαι ‘as many as’ goes with ἔσαν, the epic form of ἦσαν ‘were’. ἀριστήων is the genitive plural of ἀριστεύς ‘best man, chief’, the great men of the heroic age.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἀμφ’ αἷμα κελαινὸν ἀολλέες ἠγερέθοντο,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ βούλευον ὅπως ἐρέοιμι ἑκάστην.
sentences.l:
and they around the dark blood in throngs were gathering,
but I was planning how I might question each.
sentences.i: They gathered in throngs around the dark blood, and I was planning how I might question each of them.
sentences.n: The dead gather round the dark blood, and Odysseus’ plan in the next lines turns on it. αἷμα κελαινόν is ‘the dark blood’. ἀολλέες is ‘in a crowd, all together’. ἠγερέθοντο is ‘they were gathering’, an extended imperfect of ἀγείρω. βούλευον is ‘I was planning’, and ὅπως ἐρέοιμι is ‘how I might question’, with an optative after a past tense. ἑκάστην is ‘each’ (feminine, each of the women).

sentences.t: ἥδε δέ μοι κατὰ θυμὸν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή·
sentences.l: And this, for me, in my heart, appeared the best plan.
sentences.i: And this plan seemed best to me in my heart.
sentences.n: What Odysseus does next: he lets the women come to the blood one at a time. The line is the one at 9.318, where he was planning against the Cyclops, and it has the same English; there it ends with a full stop, and here an ano teleia stands because the plan follows. ἥδε is ‘this’, pointing forward to the plan. μοι κατὰ θυμόν is ‘for me, in my heart’; φαίνετο is ‘appeared’; ἀρίστη βουλή is ‘the best plan’.

sentences.t:
σπασσάμενος τανύηκες ἄορ παχέος παρὰ μηροῦ
οὐκ εἴων πίνειν ἅμα πάσας αἷμα κελαινόν.
sentences.l:
drawing the long-pointed sword from beside my stout thigh,
I did not allow them all to drink the dark blood together.
sentences.i: Drawing the long-pointed sword from beside my stout thigh, I would not let them all drink the dark blood at once.
sentences.n: This is the plan: with his sword drawn he keeps the women from drinking all at once. The first line stands also at 10.439, and has the English it has there. σπασσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of σπάω ‘draw’. τανύηκες ‘long-pointed’ (ἀκ- is ‘point’, as in πυριήκης) agrees with ἄορ ‘sword’; παχέος is ‘stout’, of the thigh. οὐκ εἴων is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, ‘I was not allowing’. ἅμα πάσας is ‘all together, at the same time’.

sentences.t:
αἱ δὲ προμνηστῖναι ἐπήισαν, ἠδὲ ἑκάστη
ὃν γόνον ἐξαγόρευεν·
sentences.l:
and they one after another came forward, and each
her own descent was declaring;
sentences.i: They came forward one after another, and each of them told her own descent;
sentences.n: The women come up in turn, and each says who begot her. προμνηστῖναι is an adverb, ‘one after another, in order’; it is a rare word and its sense is taken from the context. ἐπήισαν is the imperfect of ἔπειμι ‘come on, approach’. ὃν γόνον is ‘her own descent’: ὅς here is the possessive ‘her own’, easily mistaken for the relative, and γόνος is ‘birth, lineage’. ἐξαγόρευεν is ‘was declaring’. The unit stops in the middle of line 234, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δ’ ἐρέεινον ἁπάσας.
sentences.l: and I questioned them all.
sentences.i: and I questioned them all.
sentences.n: This half-line is a sentence of its own. ἐρέεινον is ‘I questioned’, the imperfect of ἐρεείνω, a verb of asking related to the ἐρέοιμι of 229; the English keeps ‘question’ for both. ἁπάσας is ‘all’, an intensified πάσας.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι πρώτην Τυρὼ ἴδον εὐπατέρειαν,
ἣ φάτο Σαλμωνῆος ἀμύμονος ἔκγονος εἶναι,
φῆ δὲ Κρηθῆος γυνὴ ἔμμεναι Αἰολίδαο·
sentences.i: There I saw Tyro first, the daughter of a good father, who said that she was the child of blameless Salmoneus and the wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus;
sentences.n: The catalogue of women begins, and each woman is introduced much the same way: ‘her I saw’, then who she was. Tyro comes first. ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι is ‘there, truly’. εὐπατέρεια is ‘well-fathered, of a good father’ (ἐύ ‘good’ + πατήρ), an epithet for a woman of good family. ἴδον, φάτο and φῆ are unaugmented (Attic εἶδον, ἔφατο, ἔφη); ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι). ἀμύμων is the stock ‘blameless’, but what it really meant is not known; the English follows the traditional guess. Αἰολίδαο ‘son of Aeolus’ is a patronymic in the epic genitive -αο; Κρηθῆος is the genitive of Κρηθεύς.

sentences.t:
ἣ ποταμοῦ ἠράσσατ’ Ἐνιπῆος θείοιο,
ὃς πολὺ κάλλιστος ποταμῶν ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἵησι,
καί ῥ’ ἐπ’ Ἐνιπῆος πωλέσκετο καλὰ ῥέεθρα.
sentences.l:
who loved the river Enipeus, the divine,
who by far the fairest of rivers over the earth sends (his stream),
and to Enipeus’ fine streams she used to go.
sentences.i: She loved the divine river Enipeus, who sends his stream over the earth, by far the most beautiful of rivers, and she used to go to the fine streams of the Enipeus.
sentences.n: Tyro’s love for a river is what the god uses. ἠράσσατο is the aorist of ἐράομαι ‘love’, with the genitive; θείοιο is the epic genitive of θεῖος ‘divine’. ὃς … ἵησι: ἵησι is ‘sends’, with its object, the stream, understood, and ποταμῶν is partitive, ‘of rivers’; πολὺ κάλλιστος is ‘by far the fairest’. πωλέσκετο has the iterative ending -σκ-, ‘she used to go’, with ἐπί and the accusative meaning ‘to’. καλά, ‘fine’, is the plain καλός. καί ῥ’ is καὶ ῥα, ‘and so’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρα εἰσάμενος γαιήοχος ἐννοσίγαιος
ἐν προχοῇς ποταμοῦ παρελέξατο δινήεντος·
sentences.l:
And, like to him having made himself, the earth-holder, the earth-shaker,
at the mouths of the eddying river lay beside her;
sentences.i: Then the earth-holder, the earth-shaker, took the likeness of the river and lay with her at the mouths of the eddying river;
sentences.n: Poseidon appears, named only by two epithets: γαιήοχος ‘earth-holder’ and ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’ (the second is built on γαῖα ‘earth’, as the more usual ἐνοσίχθων is built on χθών). τῷ … εἰσάμενος is ‘making himself like him’: εἰσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of εἴδομαι ‘make oneself like’, and the dative τῷ names the one he imitates, the river. ἐν προχοῇς is ‘at the mouths’, προχοαί being the places where a river pours out. παρελέξατο is the aorist middle of παραλέγομαι, ‘lay beside, lay with’, the plain verb for sleeping with someone. δινήεντος is ‘eddying’, from δίνη ‘eddy’.

sentences.t:
πορφύρεον δ’ ἄρα κῦμα περιστάθη, οὔρεϊ ἶσον,
κυρτωθέν, κρύψεν δὲ θεὸν θνητήν τε γυναῖκα.
sentences.l:
And a surging wave then stood around, equal to a mountain,
arched, and hid the god and the mortal woman.
sentences.i: Then a surging wave stood around them, as high as a mountain, arching over, and hid the god and the mortal woman.
sentences.n: The wave makes a private chamber for the two: it stands around them like a wall and arches over. πορφύρεον is literally ‘dark-gleaming, surging’ (the same root that gives ‘purple’); of water it describes the heave and shine of the wave, not a colour, and the English keeps ‘surging’, as at 2.428. περιστάθη is the aorist passive of περιίστημι, here ‘stood around’. οὔρεϊ is the epic dative of ὄρος ‘mountain’, taken by ἶσον ‘equal to’. κυρτωθέν is the aorist passive participle of κυρτόω ‘curve, bend’. κρύψεν is ἔκρυψε without the augment, from κρύπτω ‘hide’. θεόν and θνητὴν γυναῖκα set ‘god’ against ‘mortal woman’.

sentences.t: λῦσε δὲ παρθενίην ζώνην, κατὰ δ’ ὕπνον ἔχευεν.
sentences.l: And he loosed her maiden girdle, and down sleep he poured.
sentences.i: He loosed her maiden’s girdle and poured sleep over her.
sentences.n: Loosing the girdle is the plain way of saying that the girl has been taken; the sleep is poured on her at the same moment. λῦσε is ἔλυσε without the augment. παρθενίην ζώνην is ‘her maiden girdle’, the belt of a girl who has not yet lain with a man. κατὰ … ἔχευεν is tmesis for κατέχευεν ‘poured down’, from χέω ‘pour’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐτέλεσσε θεὸς φιλοτήσια ἔργα,
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρί, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
But when then the god had accomplished the works of love,
he clasped her by the hand, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: When the god had finished the works of love, he took her hand and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: The second line is a formula, also at 2.301–302 (where Antinous takes Telemachus by the hand), and has the English it has there, with ‘her’ for οἱ. ἐτέλεσσε is ‘accomplished’, with the doubled σ; φιλοτήσια ἔργα are ‘the works of love’. ἔν … φῦ is tmesis for ἐνέφυ, ‘grew into, took firm hold of’, and οἱ is ‘to her’; χειρί is ‘by the hand’. ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is ἐξονόμαζε, ‘addressed by name’; although the god never says her name here, ‘calling by name’ is the fixed phrase for addressing someone.

sentences.t: χαῖρε, γύναι, φιλότητι·
sentences.l: ‘Be glad, woman, in love;
sentences.i: ‘Be glad of this love, woman;
sentences.n: Poseidon’s speech runs to the end of 252. χαῖρε is the imperative of χαίρω; as a greeting it is ‘welcome, hail’ or ‘farewell’, but with the dative φιλότητι ‘in love’ it keeps its root sense, ‘be glad’. γύναι is the vocative of γυνή, the plain address ‘woman’, with no title. φιλότης is ‘love’, here the love of the bed. The unit stops in the middle of line 248, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
περιπλομένου δ’ ἐνιαυτοῦ
τέξεις ἀγλαὰ τέκνα, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἀποφώλιοι εὐναὶ
ἀθανάτων·
sentences.i: When the year comes round you will bear splendid children, for the beds of the immortals are not fruitless;
sentences.n: Poseidon promises children. περιπλομένου … ἐνιαυτοῦ is a genitive absolute, ‘as the year goes round’, from a shortened (syncopated) form of περιπέλομαι ‘revolve’; so the children are born a year later. τέξεις is the future of τίκτω ‘bear’; ἀγλαά is ‘splendid’. ἀποφώλιοι is ‘fruitless, vain’: the sense is clear from the context, but where the word comes from is not known. εὐναί are ‘beds’ and ἀθανάτων is ‘of immortals’: a god’s union is never without result.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ τοὺς κομέειν ἀτιταλλέμεναί τε.
sentences.l: and you are to tend and rear them.
sentences.i: and you must tend and rear them.
sentences.n: The infinitives κομέειν and ἀτιταλλέμεναι stand for commands: ‘you are to tend and rear’. κομέειν is the open form of κομεῖν ‘look after’, and ἀτιταλλέμεναι is the epic infinitive in -μεναι of ἀτιτάλλω ‘foster, rear’. τούς is a pronoun, ‘them’, not an article. This half-line is a sentence of its own.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἔρχευ πρὸς δῶμα, καὶ ἴσχεο μηδ’ ὀνομήνῃς·
sentences.l: But now go to your home, and restrain yourself, and do not mention (it);
sentences.i: But now go to your house, and restrain yourself, and do not mention it;
sentences.n: He sends her home with an order of silence. ἔρχευ is the imperative of ἔρχομαι. ἴσχεο is the imperative of ἴσχω in the middle voice, ‘hold yourself back, restrain yourself’. μηδ’ ὀνομήνῃς is a prohibition (μή with an aorist subjunctive) from ὀνομαίνω ‘name, mention’. No object is given: she is not to speak of what has happened, and the next line, in which the god gives his own name, shows what she is probably not to reveal. πρὸς δῶμα is ‘to the house’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοί εἰμι Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων.
sentences.l: but I, you must know, am Poseidon earth-shaker.’
sentences.i: But I, you must know, am Poseidon earth-shaker.’
sentences.n: The god gives his name last, as the reason for silence. αὐτάρ is ‘but’. τοί may be read as σοι ‘to you’ or as the particle ‘surely’; the English ‘you must know’ keeps the force of pointing. εἰμι is ‘I am’, and Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is the god’s name with its stock epithet ‘earth-shaker’. His speech, and the single quotation marks, end here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὑπὸ πόντον ἐδύσετο κυμαίνοντα.
sentences.l: So speaking, beneath the surging sea he sank down.
sentences.i: So speaking, he sank down beneath the surging sea.
sentences.n: The god leaves the way he came. The line is the one at 4.570, and has the English it already has. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, an aorist participle. ἐδύσετο is the aorist of δύω ‘sink, go down’, in the epic form with -σε-. κυμαίνοντα is ‘surging’, from κῦμα ‘wave’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὑποκυσαμένη Πελίην τέκε καὶ Νηλῆα,
τὼ κρατερὼ θεράποντε Διὸς μεγάλοιο γενέσθην
ἀμφοτέρω·
sentences.i: She conceived and bore Pelias and Neleus, and both of them became strong attendants of great Zeus;
sentences.n: Tyro’s sons by Poseidon. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’. ὑποκυσαμένη is the aorist participle of ὑποκύω ‘conceive’ (ὑπο- ‘under’). Πελίην and Νηλῆα are accusatives of Πελίης and Νηλεύς. τὼ κρατερὼ θεράποντε … γενέσθην is dual: ‘the two became strong attendants’, with ἀμφοτέρω ‘both’ closing the thought. θεράποντες are attendants, men who serve; Homer does not say what service. μεγάλοιο is ‘great’, in the epic genitive -οιο. The unit stops in the middle of line 256.

sentences.t:
Πελίης μὲν ἐν εὐρυχόρῳ Ἰαωλκῷ
ναῖε πολύρρηνος, ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν Πύλῳ ἠμαθόεντι.
sentences.l:
Pelias, on the one hand, in Iolcus of wide dancing-grounds
dwelt, rich in sheep, and the other in sandy Pylos.
sentences.i: Pelias lived in spacious Iolcus, rich in sheep, and the other in sandy Pylos.
sentences.n: The two sons go separate ways. The unit begins in the middle of line 256. ναῖε is ‘dwelt’, the imperfect of ναίω without the augment, and it serves both halves of the sentence: ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐν Πύλῳ (‘and the other, in Pylos’) leaves it to be understood. εὐρυχόρῳ is ‘of wide dancing-grounds’ (εὐρύς ‘wide’ + χορός), English ‘spacious’. πολύρρηνος is ‘rich in sheep’ (πολύς + ῥήν ‘lamb, sheep’), built like πολύχρυσος ‘rich in gold’. Πύλῳ ἠμαθόεντι is ‘sandy Pylos’, from ἄμαθος ‘sand’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἑτέρους Κρηθῆι τέκεν βασίλεια γυναικῶν,
Αἴσονά τ’ ἠδὲ Φέρητ’ Ἀμυθάονά θ’ ἱππιοχάρμην.
sentences.l:
and the others to Cretheus she bore, the queen of women,
Aeson and Pheres and Amythaon, the chariot-fighter.
sentences.i: The queen of women bore other sons to Cretheus: Aeson and Pheres and Amythaon, the chariot-fighter.
sentences.n: Tyro’s second family, by her husband. ἑτέρους is ‘others, a second set’ (the first pair were Poseidon’s), and Κρηθῆι is the dative of Κρηθεύς, ‘to Cretheus’. βασίλεια γυναικῶν is ‘queen of women’, Tyro again, the subject of τέκεν ‘bore’ (unaugmented). Αἴσονα, Φέρητα and Ἀμυθάονα are accusatives. ἱππιοχάρμην is ‘chariot-fighter’ (ἵππιος ‘of horses’ + χάρμη ‘battle’) and belongs to the last name.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ μετ’ Ἀντιόπην ἴδον, Ἀσωποῖο θύγατρα,
ἣ δὴ καὶ Διὸς εὔχετ’ ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσιν ἰαῦσαι,
καί ῥ’ ἔτεκεν δύο παῖδ’, Ἀμφίονά τε Ζῆθόν τε,
sentences.l:
And after her Antiope I saw, the daughter of Asopus,
who indeed also declared that she had slept in the arms of Zeus,
and she bore two sons, Amphion and Zethus,
sentences.i: Next after her I saw Antiope, the daughter of Asopus, who declared that she had slept in the arms of Zeus, and she bore two sons, Amphion and Zethus,
sentences.n: Antiope, the next of the women; she is introduced by τὴν δὲ μετ’ … ἴδον, ‘and after her I saw’, a pattern that returns at 266 and 305, with μετά and the accusative meaning ‘after’. Ἀσωποῖο is the epic genitive of Ἀσωπός ‘Asopus’. εὔχετ’ is εὔχετο ‘declared’: εὔχομαι means ‘pray’ and also ‘declare, claim’. ἰαῦσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἰαύω ‘sleep, lie’, and ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσιν is ‘in the arms’ (dative -ῃσιν). δύο παῖδ’ is ‘two sons’ (παῖς is ‘child, son’). The sentence runs six lines, so it is cut here, at a comma.

sentences.t:
οἳ πρῶτοι Θήβης ἕδος ἔκτισαν ἑπταπύλοιο,
πύργωσάν τ’, ἐπεὶ οὐ μὲν ἀπύργωτόν γ’ ἐδύναντο
ναιέμεν εὐρύχορον Θήβην, κρατερώ περ ἐόντε.
sentences.l:
who first the seat of Thebes founded, the seven-gated,
and gave it towers, since not indeed without towers were they able
to live in Thebes of wide dancing-grounds, strong though they were.
sentences.i: They were the first to found the seat of seven-gated Thebes, and they gave it towers, for they could not live in spacious Thebes without towers, strong as they were.
sentences.n: The two brothers found Thebes, and the point is that even strong men need walls. Θήβης ἕδος is ‘the seat, the foundation, of Thebes’; ἑπταπύλοιο is ‘seven-gated’ (ἑπτά + πύλη). πύργωσαν is the aorist of πυργόω ‘furnish with towers’ (πύργος ‘tower’), without the augment; ἀπύργωτον is its negative adjective, ‘without towers’. οὐ μέν … γε is ‘assuredly not’. ἐδύναντο is ‘they were able’ and ναιέμεν the epic infinitive of ναίω ‘dwell’. εὐρύχορον is ‘of wide dancing-grounds’, as in 256. κρατερώ περ ἐόντε is dual, ‘strong though they were’, with περ meaning ‘although’.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ μετ’ Ἀλκμήνην ἴδον, Ἀμφιτρύωνος ἄκοιτιν,
ἥ ῥ’ Ἡρακλῆα θρασυμέμνονα θυμολέοντα
γείνατ’ ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσι Διὸς μεγάλοιο μιγεῖσα·
sentences.i: Next after her I saw Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon, who bore Heracles, bold of purpose and lion-hearted, when she lay in the arms of great Zeus;
sentences.n: The mother of Heracles. The introduction is the same, τὴν δὲ μετ’ … ἴδον. ἄκοιτιν is ‘wife’. γείνατ’ is γείνατο ‘bore’, the aorist of γείνομαι, unaugmented. Ἡρακλῆα is the epic accusative of Ἡρακλῆς. θρασυμέμνονα is ‘bold of purpose’: the second half is probably from μέμονα ‘be eager, intend’, but the formation is not certain and ‘bold of purpose’ is the usual gloss. θυμολέοντα is ‘lion-hearted’ (θυμός ‘heart’ + λέων ‘lion’). μιγεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of μίγνυμι, used like a middle: ‘having lain with’; ἐν ἀγκοίνῃσι Διὸς μεγάλοιο is ‘in the arms of great Zeus’, the phrase used of Antiope, there without μεγάλοιο.

sentences.t:
καὶ Μεγάρην, Κρείοντος ὑπερθύμοιο θύγατρα,
τὴν ἔχεν Ἀμφιτρύωνος υἱὸς μένος αἰὲν ἀτειρής.
sentences.l:
and Megara, the daughter of high-spirited Creon,
whom had the son of Amphitryon, in strength ever unwearied.
sentences.i: and Megara, the daughter of high-spirited Creon, whom the son of Amphitryon had as his wife, ever unwearied in strength.
sentences.n: Heracles’ wife. Μεγάρην is the accusative ‘Megara’, joined to Alcmene as one more woman seen. Κρείοντος is the genitive of Κρείων, the name ‘Creon’; ὑπερθύμοιο is ‘high-spirited’. τὴν ἔχεν is ‘whom he had’, as a wife, with ἔχεν for εἶχε. Ἀμφιτρύωνος υἱός is Heracles by periphrasis, the son of Alcmene’s human husband, and Homer does not name him. μένος … ἀτειρής is ‘unwearied in strength’: ἀτειρής ‘not worn down’ (ἀ- + τείρω ‘wear’), and μένος ‘strength’ is an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
μητέρα τ’ Οἰδιπόδαο ἴδον, καλὴν Ἐπικάστην,
ἣ μέγα ἔργον ἔρεξεν ἀιδρείῃσι νόοιο
γημαμένη ᾧ υἷι·
sentences.i: And I saw the mother of Oedipus, beautiful Epicaste, who did a great deed in the ignorance of her mind, marrying her own son;
sentences.n: Epicaste, the woman whom later writers call Jocasta. Οἰδιπόδαο is the genitive of Οἰδίπους, ‘Oedipus’. ἀιδρείῃσι νόοιο is ‘in the ignorance of her mind’: ἀιδρείη is ‘ignorance, not knowing’ (from ἴδμεν ‘know’), a plural for a single state, and νόος is ‘mind’; the point is that she did not know. γημαμένη ᾧ υἷι is ‘having married her own son’: ᾧ is the possessive ‘her own’, υἷι is the dative of υἱός, and γημαμένη is the aorist middle participle, the form for a woman who marries. μέγα ἔργον is ‘a great deed’, here a terrible one. The unit stops in the middle of line 273.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ὃν πατέρ’ ἐξεναρίξας
γῆμεν·
sentences.l:
and he, his own father having killed,
married (her);
sentences.i: and he killed his own father and married her;
sentences.n: The other half of the horror; the unit begins in the middle of line 273. ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, Oedipus; ὃν πατέρ’ is ‘his own father’, with the possessive ὅς. ἐξεναρίξας is the aorist participle of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill, strip of arms’. γῆμεν is the unaugmented aorist ‘he married’ (ἔγημε), the verb used of a man, so the woman is ‘her’, understood. The unit ends in the middle of line 274, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἄφαρ δ’ ἀνάπυστα θεοὶ θέσαν ἀνθρώποισιν.
sentences.l: and at once the gods made (it) known to men.
sentences.i: and the gods at once made it known to men.
sentences.n: The crime is brought to light. ἄφαρ is ‘at once’. ἀνάπυστα is an adjective, ‘found out, made known’ (from ἀναπυνθάνομαι), and with θέσαν ‘made’ (ἔθεσαν, without the augment) it means ‘made (it) known’; ἀνθρώποισιν is ‘to men’. In this account the gods are the ones who reveal it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἐν Θήβῃ πολυηράτῳ ἄλγεα πάσχων
Καδμείων ἤνασσε θεῶν ὀλοὰς διὰ βουλάς·
sentences.l:
But he, in much-loved Thebes, suffering pains,
ruled the Cadmeans through the gods’ deadly plans;
sentences.i: But he went on ruling the Cadmeans in beloved Thebes, suffering pains, because of the deadly plans of the gods;
sentences.n: Oedipus stays king, in pain. ὁ μέν … begins a contrast that ἡ δ’ answers in 277. ἄλγεα πάσχων is ‘suffering pains’. Καδμείων is ‘of the Cadmeans’, the Thebans, and the genitive depends on ἤνασσε ‘ruled’ (ἀνάσσω takes the genitive). πολυηράτῳ is ‘much-loved’ (πολύς + ἐράω). In θεῶν ὀλοὰς διὰ βουλάς the preposition διά stands between the adjective and its noun; it means ‘through, by reason of’, and βουλάς are ‘plans’, as in 230. ὀλοάς is ‘deadly’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἔβη εἰς Ἀίδαο πυλάρταο κρατεροῖο,
ἁψαμένη βρόχον αἰπὺν ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῖο μελάθρου,
ᾧ ἄχεϊ σχομένη·
sentences.i: but she went to the house of Hades, the strong gate-fastener, having fastened a steep noose from the high roof-beam, gripped by her own grief;
sentences.n: Epicaste hangs herself; Odysseus says it plainly. εἰς Ἀίδαο is ‘to (the house) of Hades’, ‘house’ being understood. πυλάρταο is the epic genitive of πυλάρτης; its meaning is not certain, and the English follows the traditional explanation, ‘who fastens the gates’ (πύλη ‘gate’ and a verb of fastening). κρατεροῖο is ‘strong’. ἁψαμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἅπτω ‘fasten’, and βρόχον αἰπύν is ‘a steep noose’, with the house word for αἰπύς, here of a rope that hangs a long way down. ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῖο μελάθρου is ‘from the high roof-beam’. ᾧ ἄχεϊ σχομένη is ‘gripped by her own grief’ (aorist middle participle of ἔχω; ᾧ the possessive). The unit stops in the middle of line 279.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄλγεα κάλλιπ’ ὀπίσσω
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα τε μητρὸς Ἐρινύες ἐκτελέουσιν.
sentences.l:
but to him pains she left behind,
very many, as many as a mother’s Erinyes bring to pass.
sentences.i: but she left him very many pains behind, as many as a mother’s Erinyes bring to pass.
sentences.n: Her death passes the pain to her son. The unit begins in the middle of line 279. κάλλιπ’ is κατέλιπε, ‘she left’, with κατά shortened to κάλ- before the λ and the last vowel dropped; ὀπίσσω is ‘behind, after’. ὅσσα τε is ‘as many as’, with the epic τε of general statements. Ἐρινύες are the Erinyes, the avenging spirits who enforce a mother’s claims; ‘a mother’s Erinyes’ are the ones her wrongs call up. ἐκτελέουσιν is ‘they bring to pass’, an open form of ἐκτελέω.

sentences.t:
καὶ Χλῶριν εἶδον περικαλλέα, τήν ποτε Νηλεὺς
γῆμεν ἑὸν διὰ κάλλος, ἐπεὶ πόρε μυρία ἕδνα,
ὁπλοτάτην κούρην Ἀμφίονος Ἰασίδαο,
ὅς ποτ’ ἐν Ὀρχομενῷ Μινυείῳ ἶφι ἄνασσεν·
sentences.l:
And Chloris I saw, very fair, whom once Neleus
married because of her own beauty, since he gave numberless bridal gifts,
the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus,
who once in Minyan Orchomenus ruled with force;
sentences.i: And I saw Chloris, very fair, whom Neleus once married for her own beauty, after giving countless bridal gifts, the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus, who once ruled powerfully in Minyan Orchomenus;
sentences.n: Chloris, the wife of Neleus, the king of Pylos, and the mother of the children in the next lines. εἶδον is ‘I saw’, with the augment. περικαλλέα is ‘very fair’. γῆμεν is the same ‘married’ as in 274. ἑὸν διὰ κάλλος is ‘because of her own beauty’: ἑόν is the possessive ‘her own’, and διά follows it. πόρε is ‘gave’ (ἔπορε) and ἕδνα are the gifts a suitor gives the bride’s family; μυρία is ‘countless’. ὁπλοτάτην is ‘youngest’. Ἀμφίονος Ἰασίδαο is ‘Amphion, son of Iasus’; this Amphion is king of Orchomenus, not the Theban builder of 262. ἶφι ἄνασσεν is ‘ruled with force’: ἶφι is an old instrumental of ἴς ‘force’, and ἄνασσεν is ἤνασσε without the augment. Μινυείῳ is ‘Minyan’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ Πύλου βασίλευε, τέκεν δέ οἱ ἀγλαὰ τέκνα,
Νέστορά τε Χρόμιον τε Περικλύμενόν τ’ ἀγέρωχον.
sentences.l:
and she was queen of Pylos, and bore to him splendid children,
Nestor and Chromius and Periclymenus the lofty.
sentences.i: She was queen of Pylos and bore him splendid children: Nestor, Chromius, and lofty Periclymenus.
sentences.n: Chloris’ children. βασίλευε is ‘was queen’, with the genitive Πύλου ‘over Pylos’. τέκεν is ‘bore’ without the augment, and οἱ is ‘to him’, to Neleus. ἀγλαά is ‘splendid’. Νέστορα, Χρόμιον and Περικλύμενον are accusatives. ἀγέρωχον is an epithet of unknown meaning; ‘proud’, ‘lofty’ and ‘honoured’ have all been guessed, and the English keeps ‘lofty’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἐπ’ ἰφθίμην Πηρὼ τέκε, θαῦμα βροτοῖσι,
τὴν πάντες μνώοντο περικτίται·
sentences.l:
And after them she bore mighty Pero, a wonder to mortals,
whom all the neighbours were wooing;
sentences.i: After them she bore mighty Pero, a wonder to mortals, whom all the neighbours were wooing;
sentences.n: Pero, the daughter, and the problem she causes. τοῖσι δ’ ἐπί is ‘and after these’ (ἐπί with the dative: ‘in addition to’). ἰφθίμην is ‘mighty’; θαῦμα βροτοῖσι is ‘a wonder to mortals’. μνώοντο is ‘were wooing’, the imperfect of μνάομαι in its epic form, and περικτίται are ‘neighbours, those who live round about’. The unit stops in the middle of line 288, at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Νηλεὺς
τῷ ἐδίδου ὃς μὴ ἕλικας βόας εὐρυμετώπους
ἐκ Φυλάκης ἐλάσειε βίης Ἰφικληείης
ἀργαλέας·
sentences.i: and Neleus would give her to no one who did not drive off the cattle of crumpled horn and broad brow, those grievous cattle, from Phylace, from the strong figure of Iphicles;
sentences.n: Neleus sets an impossible price: the cattle of Iphicles. The unit begins and ends in the middle of a line. οὐδ’ ἄρα is ‘and then not’, and ἐδίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘would give’. τῷ is a pronoun, ‘to him’, and ὃς μὴ … ἐλάσειε is a relative clause with an optative: ‘to anyone who did not drive off’, ἐλάσειε being the aorist optative of ἐλαύνω. ἕλικας βόας are ‘crumple-horned cattle’ (ἕλιξ ‘twisted, curved’, of horns) and εὐρυμετώπους is ‘broad-browed’. Φυλάκης is Phylace, a town. βίης Ἰφικληείης is a periphrasis, ‘the force of Iphicles’, in place of the bare name. ἀργαλέας is the stock ‘grievous’: of cattle it says that they are hard to deal with.

sentences.t:
τὰς δ’ οἶος ὑπέσχετο μάντις ἀμύμων
ἐξελάαν·
sentences.l:
and these, alone, promised the seer, blameless,
to drive out;
sentences.i: and the blameless seer alone promised to drive them out;
sentences.n: One man alone will try. τάς is ‘these’, a pronoun for the cattle. οἶος is ‘alone’. ὑπέσχετο is ‘promised, undertook’, the aorist middle of ὑπισχνέομαι. ἐξελάαν is the infinitive of ἐξελαύνω, ‘to drive out’, with its vowels left open. μάντις is ‘seer’; ἀμύμων is the stock ‘blameless’, whose true meaning is not known. The seer is not named here. The unit begins and ends in the middle of a line.

sentences.t:
χαλεπὴ δὲ θεοῦ κατὰ μοῖρα πέδησε,
δεσμοί τ’ ἀργαλέοι καὶ βουκόλοι ἀγροιῶται.
sentences.l:
but a harsh fate of a god fettered (him) fast,
and grievous bonds and cowherds, countrymen.
sentences.i: but the harsh fate of a god fettered him, with grievous bonds and cowherds from the countryside.
sentences.n: The attempt fails: the seer is caught. The unit begins in the middle of line 292. χαλεπή is ‘harsh’ (as in ‘harsh old age’) and μοῖρα is ‘fate’, a portion dealt out by an unnamed god (θεοῦ). κατὰ … πέδησε is tmesis for κατεπέδησε, ‘fettered fast’ (πεδάω ‘fetter’). δεσμοί ‘bonds’ and βουκόλοι ‘cowherds’, with ἀγροιῶται ‘countrymen’, belong to the subject: the harsh fate came in the form of bonds and herdsmen. ἀργαλέοι is ‘grievous’ again.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μῆνές τε καὶ ἡμέραι ἐξετελεῦντο
ἂψ περιτελλομένου ἔτεος καὶ ἐπήλυθον ὧραι,
καὶ τότε δή μιν ἔλυσε βίη Ἰφικληείη,
θέσφατα πάντ’ εἰπόντα·
sentences.l:
But when indeed the months and the days were completed,
as the year went round again, and the seasons came on,
then indeed him loosed the force of Iphicles,
(him) having told all the god-declared things;
sentences.i: But when the months and the days were completed, as the year came round again and the seasons came on, then the strong figure of Iphicles freed him, after he had told all the prophecies;
sentences.n: A year passes and the seer is freed. ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ is ‘but when indeed’. ἐξετελεῦντο is ‘were being completed’, the imperfect passive of ἐκτελέω. ἂψ περιτελλομένου ἔτεος is a genitive absolute, ‘the year going round again’ (ἔτος ‘year’); ἐπήλυθον is ἐπῆλθον, ‘came on’, and ὧραι are ‘seasons’. μιν is ‘him’, the seer. βίη Ἰφικληείη is the same periphrasis as in 290. θέσφατα πάντ’ εἰπόντα is ‘having told all the prophecies’: θέσφατα are things declared by a god, and εἰπόντα is the aorist participle of εἶπον, agreeing with μιν. Odysseus does not say what the prophecies were. The unit ends in the middle of line 297.

sentences.t: Διὸς δ’ ἐτελείετο βουλή.
sentences.l: and of Zeus the plan was being fulfilled.
sentences.i: and the plan of Zeus was being fulfilled.
sentences.n: A single clause that sums up the story: all of this fulfilled what Zeus had planned. The unit begins in the middle of line 297. ἐτελείετο is the imperfect passive of τελείω ‘bring to an end, fulfil’. βουλή is ‘plan’, the same word as in 230, but here it is the plan of a god.

sentences.t:
καὶ Λήδην εἶδον, τὴν Τυνδαρέου παράκοιτιν,
ἥ ῥ’ ὑπὸ Τυνδαρέῳ κρατερόφρονε γείνατο παῖδε,
Κάστορά θ’ ἱππόδαμον καὶ πὺξ ἀγαθὸν Πολυδεύκεα,
τοὺς ἄμφω ζωοὺς κατέχει φυσίζοος αἶα·
sentences.l:
And Leda I saw, the wife of Tyndareus,
who to Tyndareus bore two sons, strong-minded,
Castor, horse-taming, and Polydeuces, good with the fist,
both of whom, alive, the life-giving earth holds fast;
sentences.i: And I saw Leda, the wife of Tyndareus, who bore to Tyndareus two sons of strong mind, Castor, tamer of horses, and Polydeuces, good with his fists, both of whom the life-giving earth holds fast, though they are alive;
sentences.n: Leda and her two sons. καὶ Λήδην εἶδον is ‘and Leda I saw’. ὑπὸ Τυνδαρέῳ is ‘to Tyndareus’ (a woman bears a child ‘under’ her husband). γείνατο is ‘bore’. κρατερόφρονε is dual and agrees with παῖδε ‘two sons’, not with Tyndareus: ‘strong-minded’ (κρατερός + φρήν). Κάστορά θ’ ἱππόδαμον is ‘Castor, horse-taming’, and πὺξ ἀγαθόν is ‘good with the fist’, a boxer. τοὺς ἄμφω ζωούς is ‘both of whom, alive’, with ζωούς ‘living’ agreeing with τούς as a predicate. κατέχει is ‘holds fast’: they are under the earth and yet alive. φυσίζοος is ‘life-giving’, from φύσις and ζωή.

sentences.t:
οἳ καὶ νέρθεν γῆς τιμὴν πρὸς Ζηνὸς ἔχοντες
ἄλλοτε μὲν ζώουσ’ ἑτερήμεροι, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
τεθνᾶσιν·
sentences.i: who, even beneath the earth, have honour from Zeus: at one time they live on alternate days, at another they are dead;
sentences.n: The two brothers have a strange afterlife, in which they alternate between life and death. νέρθεν γῆς is ‘from beneath the earth, below’, with the genitive. τιμήν is ‘honour’; πρὸς Ζηνός is ‘from Zeus’ (πρός with the genitive can mean ‘from the side of’, and Ζηνός is the epic genitive of Ζεύς). ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε is ‘at one time … at another again’. ζώουσ’ is ζώουσι, ‘they live’, and ἑτερήμεροι is ‘on alternate days’ (ἕτερος + ἡμέρα), and the text does not say how the two share the days; τεθνᾶσιν is ‘they are dead’, a perfect. The unit stops in the middle of line 304.

sentences.t: τιμὴν δὲ λελόγχασιν ἶσα θεοῖσι.
sentences.l: and honour they have received as their lot, equal to gods.
sentences.i: and they have received honour equal to that of gods.
sentences.n: The reward for that arrangement. The unit begins in the middle of line 304. τιμήν is ‘honour’, the word of 302 again. λελόγχασιν is the perfect of λαγχάνω, ‘have received as one’s share’; ἶσα is a neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘on a par with’, with the dative θεοῖσι ‘to gods’.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ μετ’ Ἰφιμέδειαν, Ἀλωῆος παράκοιτιν
εἴσιδον, ἣ δὴ φάσκε Ποσειδάωνι μιγῆναι,
καί ῥ’ ἔτεκεν δύο παῖδε, μινυνθαδίω δ’ ἐγενέσθην,
sentences.l:
And after her Iphimedeia, Aloeus’ wife,
I saw, who claimed to have mingled with Poseidon,
and she bore two sons, but short-lived they became,
sentences.i: Next after her I saw Iphimedeia, the wife of Aloeus, who claimed to have lain with Poseidon, and she bore two sons, but they were short-lived,
sentences.n: Iphimedeia, the mother of two giants. The sentence runs six lines, so it is cut here, at a comma. τὴν δὲ μετ’ … εἴσιδον is ‘and after her … I saw’, the object standing in the first line and the verb in the second; εἴσιδον is the aorist of εἰσοράω ‘look upon’. Ἀλωῆος is the genitive of Ἀλωεύς, ‘Aloeus’. φάσκε is ‘claimed’, the imperfect of φάσκω, and μιγῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι, ‘to have lain with’, taking the dative Ποσειδάωνι. δύο παῖδε and μινυνθαδίω … ἐγενέσθην are dual forms; μινυνθάδιος is ‘short-lived’ (μινυνθά ‘for a little while’).

sentences.t:
Ὦτόν τ’ ἀντίθεον τηλεκλειτόν τ’ Ἐφιάλτην,
οὓς δὴ μηκίστους θρέψε ζείδωρος ἄρουρα
καὶ πολὺ καλλίστους μετά γε κλυτὸν Ὠρίωνα·
sentences.i: Otus, the godlike, and far-famed Ephialtes, whom the grain-giving plough-land reared to be the tallest, and by far the most beautiful after famous Orion;
sentences.n: The earth raised the two as the tallest of all, and as the most beautiful after Orion. Ὦτον is ‘Otus’ and Ἐφιάλτην ‘Ephialtes’. ἀντίθεον is ‘godlike’; τηλεκλειτόν is ‘far-famed’ (τηλε- ‘far’ + κλειτός, a spelling of κλυτός ‘famous’). οὓς δὴ … θρέψε is ‘whom indeed … reared’, the aorist of τρέφω without the augment. ζείδωρος ἄρουρα is ‘the grain-giving plough-land’; ζείδωρος is traditionally from ζειά ‘spelt’ (a grain) and δῶρον ‘gift’, though ancient writers also took it as ‘life-giving’. μηκίστους is ‘tallest’, the superlative of μακρός ‘long’, and καλλίστους is ‘fairest’, with πολύ ‘by far’. μετά γε … is ‘after (only) famous Orion’, and κλυτόν is ‘famous’.

sentences.t:
ἐννέωροι γὰρ τοί γε καὶ ἐννεαπήχεες ἦσαν
εὖρος, ἀτὰρ μῆκός γε γενέσθην ἐννεόργυιοι.
sentences.l:
for nine years old they, indeed, and nine-cubited
in breadth were, but in length they became nine-fathomed.
sentences.i: for at nine years old they were nine cubits across, and in height they had grown to nine fathoms.
sentences.n: The giants’ measurements are for effect, not for measuring: a cubit (the forearm) is roughly 45 centimetres and a fathom (the span of two outstretched arms) roughly 1.8 metres, so nine cubits is about four metres and nine fathoms about sixteen. ἐννέωροι is ‘nine years old’. τοί γε is ‘they indeed’ (τοί is a pronoun). ἐννεαπήχεες is ‘nine cubits’ (πῆχυς ‘forearm, cubit’), and εὖρος ‘in breadth’ and μῆκος ‘in length’, here height, are accusatives of respect. ἐννεόργυιοι is ‘nine fathoms’ (ὄργυια ‘fathom’). γενέσθην is a dual aorist of γίγνομαι: ‘they became’, that is, grew to be.

sentences.t:
οἵ ῥα καὶ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀπειλήτην ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ
φυλόπιδα στήσειν πολυάικος πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
These even to the immortals in Olympus threatened
to raise the battle-din of a war of many onrushes.
sentences.i: They even threatened the immortals on Olympus that they would raise the din of a war of many onrushes.
sentences.n: Their threat against the gods. οἵ ῥα is ‘these then’ (οἵ is a pronoun, ῥα a small particle). ἀπειλήτην is the dual imperfect, ‘the two threatened’, with the dative ἀθανάτοισιν ‘to the immortals’ and the future infinitive στήσειν ‘that they would raise’ (ἵστημι ‘set up’). φυλόπιδα is ‘the din of battle’ and πολέμοιο is ‘of war’. πολυάικος is an adjective whose meaning is not certain: it is probably from ἀΐσσω ‘rush, dart’, and ‘of many onrushes’ is the traditional guess, kept here.

sentences.t:
Ὄσσαν ἐπ’ Οὐλύμπῳ μέμασαν θέμεν, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ Ὄσσῃ
Πήλιον εἰνοσίφυλλον, ἵν’ οὐρανὸς ἀμβατὸς εἴη.
sentences.l:
Ossa upon Olympus they were eager to set, and upon Ossa
Pelion, leaf-shaking, that heaven might be climbable.
sentences.i: They were eager to set Ossa upon Olympus, and upon Ossa leaf-shaking Pelion, so that heaven could be climbed.
sentences.n: What the threat was: they meant to pile the mountains into a stair to heaven. Olympus, Ossa and Pelion are real mountains of northern Greece. μέμασαν is the perfect plural of μέμονα ‘be eager, intend’, with the infinitive θέμεν (the epic form of θεῖναι), ‘to set’. εἰνοσίφυλλον is ‘leaf-shaking’ (ἔνοσις ‘shaking’ + φύλλον ‘leaf’). ἵν’ is ἵνα ‘so that’, with the optative εἴη ‘might be’, and ἀμβατός is ‘that can be climbed’, from ἀναβαίνω.

sentences.t: καί νύ κεν ἐξετέλεσσαν, εἰ ἥβης μέτρον ἵκοντο·
sentences.l: And now indeed they would have accomplished (it), if they had reached the measure of youth;
sentences.i: And they would have accomplished it, if they had reached the measure of youth;
sentences.n: A contrary-to-fact sentence: they would have done it, but they did not live long enough. καί νύ κεν ἐξετέλεσσαν is ‘and now they would have accomplished (it)’; κεν with an aorist indicative means ‘would have’. ἐξετέλεσσαν is the aorist of ἐκτελέω, with the doubled σ. εἰ … ἵκοντο is ‘if they had reached’, with an aorist indicative without its augment (Attic ἀφίκοντο), the usual form for a condition that was not met; ἥβης μέτρον is ‘the measure of youth’, full manhood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὄλεσεν Διὸς υἱός, ὃν ἠύκομος τέκε Λητώ,
ἀμφοτέρω, πρίν σφωιν ὑπὸ κροτάφοισιν ἰούλους
ἀνθῆσαι πυκάσαι τε γένυς ἐυανθέι λάχνῃ.
sentences.l:
but destroyed (them) the son of Zeus, whom fine-haired Leto bore,
both, before for the two beneath the temples the down
had bloomed and had covered their cheeks with fair-flowering beard.
sentences.i: But the son of Zeus, whom fine-haired Leto bore, destroyed them both before the down had bloomed beneath their temples and covered their cheeks with a fair-flowering beard.
sentences.n: The god kills them before they come of age. ἀλλ’ is ‘but’; ὄλεσεν is ‘destroyed’, the aorist of ὄλλυμι. Διὸς υἱός is ‘the son of Zeus’, and ὃν ἠύκομος τέκε Λητώ, ‘whom fine-haired Leto bore’, shows that it is Apollo, whom Odysseus does not name. ἀμφοτέρω is the dual ‘both’. πρίν takes the infinitives ἀνθῆσαι ‘bloom’ and πυκάσαι ‘cover thickly’: ‘before the down bloomed and covered’. σφωιν is the dual dative ‘for the two of them’, here ‘their’. ἰούλους is ‘down’, the first soft hair, and λάχνῃ, properly ‘woolly hair’, is here ‘beard’; ἐυανθέι is ‘fair-flowering’ (ἐύ + ἄνθος ‘flower’).
